topics.topic: Motion of charged particles in electric and magnetic fields

subtopics.title: Electron in a uniform electric field
subtopics.theory_md:
Electron (charge $-e$, mass $m$) in a uniform field $E$: force $F=eE$ opposite to $E$, so $a=eE/m$.
- **Accelerated through $V$:** $\tfrac12mv^2=eV$, $v=\sqrt{2eV/m}=5.93\times10^5\sqrt V$ m/s.
- **Entering perpendicular to $E$** (speed $v_0$ along $x$): $x=v_0t$, $y=\tfrac12\frac{eE}{m}t^2$, so $y=\frac{eE}{2mv_0^2}x^2$, a **parabola**. On leaving plates of length $l$: $y=\frac{eEl^2}{2mv_0^2}$, $\tan\theta=\frac{eEl}{mv_0^2}$.
- **Projected at angle $\theta$** with speed $u$ (force along $-y$): $H=\frac{mu^2\sin^2\theta}{2eE}$, $T=\frac{2mu\sin\theta}{eE}$, $R=\frac{mu^2\sin2\theta}{eE}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Same as a stone thrown in gravity: constant sideways speed, constant pull in one direction. Here the pull is $eE/m$ instead of $g$, so every projectile formula carries over with $g\to eE/m$.
key_points: Force on electron $eE$ opposite to field; $a=eE/m$ is constant
Perpendicular entry: $x=v_0t$, $y=\frac12 at^2$, parabola $y=\frac{eE}{2mv_0^2}x^2$
Oblique projection: $H=\frac{mu^2\sin^2\theta}{2eE}$, $T=\frac{2mu\sin\theta}{eE}$, $R=\frac{mu^2\sin2\theta}{eE}$
Range is maximum at $\theta=45^\circ$

questions.q: An electron accelerated through 500 V enters midway between two parallel plates, perpendicular to a uniform field $E=1.0\times10^4$ V/m. The plates are 5.0 cm long. Find the speed on entry, the deflection on leaving the plates and the angle of deviation. ($e/m=1.76\times10^{11}$ C/kg)
An electron is projected at $30^\circ$ to the $x$-axis with speed $2.0\times10^6$ m/s in a uniform field $E=1000$ V/m that pulls it back along $-y$. Find the maximum height, time of flight and range.
questions.model_answer_md:
$a=\dfrac{eE}{m}=1.76\times10^{11}\times1000=1.76\times10^{14}$ m/s$^2$

**Maximum height:** $H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2a}=\dfrac{(2\times10^6)^2(0.5)^2}{2\times1.76\times10^{14}}=2.84\times10^{-3}$ m $=2.84$ mm

**Time of flight:** $T=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{a}=\dfrac{2\times2\times10^6\times0.5}{1.76\times10^{14}}=1.14\times10^{-8}$ s

**Range:** $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{a}=\dfrac{(2\times10^6)^2\times0.866}{1.76\times10^{14}}=1.97\times10^{-2}$ m $\approx1.97$ cm

points: Force $eE$ along the field axis only; no force along the initial direction, so $x=v_0t$
Deflection at exit $\frac{eEl^2}{2mv_0^2}$ and $\tan\theta=\frac{eEl}{mv_0^2}$; straight line after leaving the field
Range $R=u\cos\theta\,T=\frac{mu^2\sin2\theta}{eE}$, maximum at $45^\circ$, path is a parabola

subtopics.title: Bethe's law: electron refraction
subtopics.theory_md:
At a surface separating regions of potential $V_1$ and $V_2$ the field is **normal** to the surface, so the **tangential velocity is unchanged**: $v_1\sin\theta_1=v_2\sin\theta_2$ (angles from the normal). With $v=\sqrt{2eV/m}\propto\sqrt V$:
$$\frac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_2}=\frac{v_2}{v_1}=\sqrt{\frac{V_2}{V_1}}$$
This is **Bethe's law**. Comparing with Snell's law $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}$, the electron refractive index is $\mu\propto\sqrt V$. Into higher potential the electron bends **towards the normal**. In a non-uniform field it holds locally; this is the basis of electron lenses. Unlike light, $\mu\propto v$, not $1/v$.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of a ball rolling over a ramp edge that only pushes it sideways-free: the push is straight across the boundary, so its sideways speed cannot change. Only the across-the-boundary speed changes, and that tilts the direction.
key_points: Field is normal to the surface, so tangential velocity is conserved: $v_1\sin\theta_1=v_2\sin\theta_2$
$v\propto\sqrt V$, hence $\sin\theta_1/\sin\theta_2=\sqrt{V_2/V_1}$
Analogy: $\mu\propto\sqrt V$, bends towards the normal into higher potential
Difference from light: $\mu\propto v$ here, whereas $\mu\propto1/v$ for light
Basis of electron lenses; holds locally in a non-uniform field

Derivation: force normal to surface, so $v_1\sin\theta_1=v_2\sin\theta_2$
Analogy: $\sqrt V$ plays the role of $\mu$, bends towards the normal into higher potential, basis of electron lenses
Bethe's law explains electron refraction at a potential boundary: tangential velocity unchanged
Comparison with Snell: $\mu\propto\sqrt V$ here, ratio is $v_2/v_1$ not $v_1/v_2$
Application: electrostatic electron lenses, microscope, CRT focusing; index can vary gradually
Field acts normal to the surface so tangential velocity is unchanged
In a non-uniform field the relation holds locally at each point; bends towards the normal into higher potential

subtopics.title: Electron in a magnetic field
subtopics.theory_md:
Force $\mathbf F=-e(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf v$: it does **no work**, so speed is constant.
- **$\mathbf v\perp\mathbf B$:** circle, $\frac{mv^2}{r}=evB\Rightarrow r=\frac{mv}{eB}=\frac1B\sqrt{\frac{2mV}{e}}$. Period $T=\frac{2\pi m}{eB}$, independent of $v$ and $r$; frequency $\frac{eB}{2\pi m}$.
- **$\mathbf v$ at angle $\phi$ to $\mathbf B$:** **helix**, radius $\frac{mv\sin\phi}{eB}$, pitch $\frac{2\pi mv\cos\phi}{eB}$.
- **Crossed $E$ and $B$:** the electron goes undeflected when $eE=evB$, i.e. $v=E/B$.
subtopics.basics_md: The magnetic push always acts sideways to the motion, like a string pulling a ball round in a circle: it turns the ball but never speeds it up. Along the field there is no push, so that part of the motion stays straight.
key_points: Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity, does no work, speed is constant
$v\perp B$: circle of radius $r=mv/eB$, period $2\pi m/eB$ independent of speed
Oblique entry: helix, pitch $2\pi mv\cos\phi/eB$
Crossed $E$ and $B$: undeflected when $v=E/B$

questions.why: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity.

questions.q: An electron accelerated through 1000 V enters a uniform magnetic field of $1.0$ mT perpendicular to its velocity. Find the radius of its circular path and its cyclotron frequency. ($e/m=1.76\times10^{11}$ C/kg)

An electron with speed $1.0\times10^7$ m/s enters a uniform field $B=2.0$ mT at $30^\circ$ to the field. Describe the path and find the radius and the pitch. ($m=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)
questions.model_answer_md:
**Path:** a **helix** along $B$: circular motion from the component $v\sin\phi$ perpendicular to $B$, uniform drift from the component $v\cos\phi$ along $B$.

**Radius:** $r=\dfrac{mv\sin\phi}{eB}=\dfrac{9.11\times10^{-31}\times10^7\times0.5}{1.60\times10^{-19}\times2\times10^{-3}}=1.42\times10^{-2}$ m $=1.42$ cm

**Pitch:** $p=v\cos\phi\cdot T=\dfrac{2\pi mv\cos\phi}{eB}=\dfrac{2\pi\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times10^7\times0.866}{1.60\times10^{-19}\times2\times10^{-3}}=0.155$ m $=15.5$ cm
points: Path is a helix (circle plus drift along $B$)

subtopics.title: Electron wavelength and resolving power
subtopics.theory_md:
Electrons accelerated through $V$ have de Broglie wavelength
$$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}=\frac{12.27}{\sqrt V}\ \text{\AA}$$
(non-relativistic). At 100 kV, $\lambda=0.0388$ Å $=3.88$ pm, about $10^5$ times shorter than visible light. The limit of resolution is $d=\frac{0.61\lambda}{\mu\sin\alpha}$, so a smaller $\lambda$ resolves finer detail. Electron microscopes reach about 0.1 to 0.2 nm; the light microscope is limited to about 200 nm. Practical limit: lens aberrations force a very small aperture $\alpha$.
subtopics.basics_md: Seeing detail is like feeling a surface with a probe: a probe thicker than the detail cannot feel it. Light waves are the thick probe; electron waves are far thinner, so they feel much finer detail.
key_points: $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2meV}=12.27/\sqrt V$ Å
Resolution $d=0.61\lambda/(\mu\sin\alpha)$: smaller $\lambda$ means better resolution
Electron $\lambda$ (picometres) is far below light $\lambda$ (hundreds of nm)
Higher accelerating voltage gives shorter $\lambda$ and higher resolution

questions.q: Find the de Broglie wavelength of electrons accelerated through 40 kV. By what factor is it shorter than green light of wavelength 550 nm? (Ignore relativistic correction.)
questions.model_answer_md:
$\lambda=\dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}=\dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{40000}}=0.0614$ Å $=6.14\times10^{-12}$ m

Factor $=\dfrac{550\times10^{-9}}{6.14\times10^{-12}}\approx9.0\times10^{4}$, so the electron wavelength is about 90 000 times shorter.

questions.q: An electron microscope uses electrons accelerated through 40 kV and has an aperture half-angle $\alpha=5\times10^{-3}$ rad in vacuum. Find the smallest separation it can resolve using $d=0.61\lambda/\sin\alpha$, and compare it with a light microscope of numerical aperture 1.4 using light of 550 nm.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Electron microscope:** $\lambda=6.14\times10^{-12}$ m (from 40 kV).
$d=\dfrac{0.61\lambda}{\sin\alpha}=\dfrac{0.61\times6.14\times10^{-12}}{5\times10^{-3}}=7.5\times10^{-10}$ m $=0.75$ nm

**Light microscope:** $d=\dfrac{0.61\times550\text{ nm}}{1.4}=240$ nm

The electron microscope resolves about $240/0.75=320$ times finer detail.
points: Electron microscope is about 320 times better

subtopics.title: Magnetic lens and electron gun
subtopics.theory_md:
**Electron gun:** heated tungsten filament (or LaB$_6$) cathode, Wehnelt cylinder (grid) to shape the beam, anode at 50 to 200 kV.

**Magnetic lens:** a short coil of $N$ turns carrying current $I$, enclosed in soft iron with a narrow gap (pole pieces). The non-uniform axial field makes electrons spiral and converge to a focus; focal length $f\propto\frac{V}{(NI)^2}$. Focusing is changed **electrically** by varying $I$, so no moving parts. A magnetic lens is always converging and rotates the image.

Everything is in a **high vacuum** so that electrons are not scattered by air.
subtopics.basics_md: A glass lens bends light because light slows in glass. An electron cannot be bent by glass, but a shaped magnetic field bends its path. More coil current gives a stronger lens and a shorter focus.
key_points: Gun: heated cathode, Wehnelt cylinder, accelerating anode (50 to 200 kV)
Magnetic lens: coil with iron pole pieces, non-uniform axial field
Focal length $f\propto V/(NI)^2$; focus is changed by varying the coil current
High vacuum avoids scattering of electrons by air molecules

questions.why: $f\propto V/(NI)^2$: more current, shorter focal length.

questions.why: Collisions with air molecules scatter and absorb the beam and burn the filament.

questions.q: Describe the electron gun and the magnetic lens of an electron microscope. How is the beam focused?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Electron gun.** A heated tungsten filament (cathode) emits electrons; a negatively biased Wehnelt cylinder shapes them into a narrow beam; the anode at a high positive potential (50 to 200 kV) accelerates them.

**Magnetic lens.** A coil of $N$ turns with current $I$ in an iron casing with a narrow pole-piece gap gives a strong, non-uniform axial magnetic field. Electrons entering at a small angle spiral and converge to a point.

**Focusing.** The focal length $f\propto V/(NI)^2$, so the beam is focused by changing the coil current $I$, with no moving parts. The whole column is evacuated.
points: Gun: heated filament cathode, Wehnelt cylinder, accelerating anode
Magnetic lens is a coil with iron pole pieces giving a non-uniform axial field
Electrons spiral and converge to a focus
Focus is changed by varying $I$ since $f\propto V/(NI)^2$

subtopics.title: Construction and working of TEM and SEM
subtopics.theory_md:
**TEM (transmission):** gun, condenser lens (illuminates the specimen), **ultra-thin specimen** (below about 100 nm), objective lens (first magnified image), intermediate and projector lenses (final image) on a fluorescent screen or CCD. Contrast comes from electrons scattered by thicker or denser regions. Magnification up to $10^6$, resolution about 0.1 nm.

**SEM (scanning):** a fine beam is scanned over the surface; **secondary electrons** emitted are collected and displayed in step with the scan. Gives a 3-D-looking surface image of thick specimens, resolution about 1 to 10 nm.
subtopics.basics_md: A TEM is like a shadow-slide projector: electrons pass through a very thin slice and are focused onto a screen. An SEM is like a finger sweeping over a surface: a tiny beam sweeps the sample and the signal is built up point by point.
key_points: TEM column: gun, condenser, specimen, objective, intermediate, projector, screen
Specimen must be ultra-thin; contrast from scattering in thicker or denser parts
SEM scans a fine beam and detects secondary electrons from the surface
TEM gives internal structure at high resolution; SEM gives surface topography of thick specimens

questions.q: In which instrument do electrons pass through the specimen to form the image?
questions.why: Transmission electron microscope; the SEM images the surface using secondary electrons.

questions.q: Which statement about the SEM is correct?
options: It forms a 3-D-like surface image from secondary electrons
questions.why: The scanned beam knocks out secondary electrons whose signal builds the image.

questions.q: Describe the construction and working of a transmission electron microscope. Why is the image formed on a fluorescent screen?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Construction** (top to bottom, in a high-vacuum column):
1. Electron gun: heated filament, Wehnelt cylinder, anode (50 to 200 kV).
2. Condenser lens: focuses the beam on the specimen.
3. Specimen: ultra-thin slice (below about 100 nm) on a copper grid.
4. Objective lens: forms the first magnified image.
5. Intermediate and projector lenses: magnify further.
6. Fluorescent screen (or CCD) at the bottom.

**Working.** The accelerated beam of wavelength $\lambda=12.27/\sqrt V$ Å passes through the specimen; denser regions scatter more electrons, giving contrast. The magnetic lenses (focused by coil current) form the final enlarged image, up to $10^6\times$, resolution about 0.1 nm.

**Screen.** The eye cannot see electrons; the fluorescent screen converts them to visible light.
points: Column in high vacuum with gun, condenser, specimen, objective, intermediate and projector lenses
All lenses are magnetic, focused by coil current
Specimen ultra-thin, contrast from differential scattering
Magnification up to $10^6$, resolution about 0.1 nm
Fluorescent screen converts electrons to visible light

questions.q: State two differences between a TEM and an SEM.
questions.model_answer_md:
| | TEM | SEM |
|---|---|---|
| Image from | Electrons transmitted through the specimen | Secondary electrons from the surface |
| Specimen | Ultra-thin | Thick allowed |
| Gives | Internal structure, resolution about 0.1 nm | Surface topography, resolution about 1 to 10 nm |
points: TEM uses transmitted electrons, SEM uses secondary electrons
TEM needs an ultra-thin specimen, SEM does not
TEM resolution is better than SEM

subtopics.title: Velocity selector (crossed E and B)
subtopics.theory_md:
Positive ions of charge $q$ move through uniform $E$ and $B$, perpendicular to each other and to the velocity. The electric force $qE$ and magnetic force $qvB$ are opposite. They balance when
$$qE=qvB\Rightarrow v=\frac EB$$
Only ions of this speed go straight through the slit; slower ions are pushed by $qE$, faster ones by $qvB$, and are stopped. The result **does not depend on $m$ or $q$**, so the exit beam is monoenergetic in speed.
subtopics.basics_md: A turnstile that opens only for walkers at one pace: too slow and one force wins and shoves you aside, too fast and the other wins. Only the exact pace passes straight.
key_points: Crossed uniform $E$ and $B$, both perpendicular to the beam
Undeflected when $qE=qvB$, so $v=E/B$
Independent of mass and charge
Other speeds are deflected and stopped by the next slit

In a velocity selector $B=0.10$ T. What electric field lets ions of speed $2.0\times10^5$ m/s pass undeflected? Which ions are deflected towards the electric-force side: faster or slower?
questions.model_answer_md:
$E=vB=2.0\times10^5\times0.10=2.0\times10^4$ V/m $=20$ kV/m

For **slower** ions $qvB<qE$, so the electric force wins and they are deflected towards the side of the electric force; faster ions are deflected the other way by the magnetic force.
points: Slower ions: electric force dominates and they are deflected out

subtopics.title: Bainbridge mass spectrograph
subtopics.theory_md:
**Principle:** ions are first made equal in speed by a velocity selector, then deflected in a uniform magnetic field into semicircles whose radius depends on mass.

**Construction:** ion source, slits $S_1,S_2$, velocity selector (plates giving $E$ plus field $B$), slit $S_3$, deflection chamber with a second field $B'$ (no $E$), photographic plate; all evacuated.

**Working:** $v=E/B$ out of the selector. In $B'$: $\frac{mv^2}{r}=qvB'\Rightarrow r=\frac{mE}{qBB'}$. Ions land at $2r$ from $S_3$, so $m=\frac{qBB'}{E}r$ and $2r\propto m$: a **linear mass scale**. Line positions give isotopic masses; line darkness gives relative abundance.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine marbles of different weight all thrown at the same speed into a circular track that bends them: the heavier ones swing out in a bigger circle. The place each lands tells its weight.
key_points: Principle: velocity selection, then semicircular deflection in $B'$
Construction: source, slits, crossed $E$ and $B$, deflection field $B'$, photographic plate
$v=E/B$ and $r=mv/qB'=mE/qBB'$
$m=\frac{qBB'}{E}r$ so $r\propto m$: linear mass scale, equally spaced lines
Line position gives mass, darkness gives abundance

questions.q: In the Bainbridge spectrograph the ions are recorded on
questions.why: The photographic plate shows one line per isotope.

questions.q: The Bainbridge mass scale is linear because
Derive the radius of the path in the Bainbridge spectrograph in terms of $E$, $B$, $B'$, $m$ and $q$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Velocity selector: $qE=qvB\Rightarrow v=\dfrac EB$.

Deflection chamber: magnetic force provides the centripetal force, $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=qvB'$, so $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB'}$.

Substituting $v$: $\boxed{r=\dfrac{mE}{qBB'}}$, so $m=\dfrac{qBB'}{E}\,r$.

points: Construction: ion source, slits, velocity selector with crossed $E$ and $B$, chamber with $B'$, photographic plate, evacuated
Isotopes land at $2r$; $m/q=BB'r/E$ so lines are separate; position gives mass, darkness gives abundance
Advantage: equal-speed ions give a linear mass scale
Principle: equal-velocity selection then deflection in uniform field
Labelled diagram: source, $S_1,S_2$, plates $P_1,P_2$ ($E$), field $B$, deflection field $B'$, photographic plate
$r\propto m$ for the same charge: lines equally spaced for integral masses, giving isotopic masses and abundances
Construction: velocity selector with $E$ and $B$, slit $S_3$, deflection field $B'$, photographic plate
Working: $v=E/B$ selected, semicircle radius from $mv^2/r=qvB'$, lands at $2r$
Proof of linear scale: $m=\frac{qBB'}{E}r$, so $m\propto r$ (and to the distance $2r$)
Hence equal mass differences give equal spacing between lines

subtopics.title: Isotope lines and mass numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
Landing distance $x=2r=\dfrac{2mE}{qBB'}$, so $x\propto\dfrac mq$.
- Separation of two isotopes of mass difference $\Delta m$ (same $q$): $\Delta x=\dfrac{2\,\Delta m\,E}{qBB'}$, the same for every $\Delta m$ of equal size.
- A doubly charged ion ($q=2e$) of mass $M$ lands where a singly charged ion of mass $M/2$ lands.
- Relative abundance is proportional to the **blackening** of the line.
Convert atomic mass units: $1\ \mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C.
subtopics.basics_md: Position on the plate is a ruler for mass per unit charge. A two-times charged ion looks half as heavy, so it can sit on top of a lighter ion's line.
key_points: Line position $x=2r=2mE/(qBB')\propto m/q$
Equal mass differences give equal separations (linear scale)
Doubly charged ion of mass $M$ falls where a singly charged ion of $M/2$ falls
Line darkness is proportional to isotopic abundance

questions.why: More ions hitting the plate blacken the line more.

questions.q: Singly ionised neon isotopes of masses 20 u and 22 u pass a Bainbridge spectrograph with $E=1.0\times10^5$ V/m, $B=0.20$ T and $B'=0.50$ T. Find the speed selected and the distance between the two lines. ($1\ \mathrm u=1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)
questions.model_answer_md:
**Speed:** $v=\dfrac EB=\dfrac{1.0\times10^5}{0.20}=5.0\times10^5$ m/s

**Positions:** $x=2r=\dfrac{2mE}{eBB'}$
- Ne-20: $x=\dfrac{2\times20\times1.66\times10^{-27}\times10^5}{1.60\times10^{-19}\times0.20\times0.50}=0.415$ m $=41.5$ cm
- Ne-22: $x=0.456$ m $=45.6$ cm

**Separation:** $\Delta x=45.6-41.5=4.1$ cm
points: Ne-20 at 41.5 cm and Ne-22 at 45.6 cm

questions.q: With the same instrument ($E=1.0\times10^5$ V/m, $B=0.20$ T, $B'=0.50$ T), doubly charged Ne-20 ions are also present. Where do they strike the plate, and which singly charged ion line do they coincide with?
questions.model_answer_md:
For $q=2e$: $x=\dfrac{2mE}{qBB'}=\dfrac{2\times20\times1.66\times10^{-27}\times10^5}{2\times1.60\times10^{-19}\times0.20\times0.50}=0.207$ m $=20.7$ cm

This equals the position of a **singly charged ion of mass 10 u**, because $x\propto m/q=20/2=10$. They would blend with any singly charged ion of mass 10 u.
points: Coincides with a singly charged 10 u ion line
